```{r}
# Part I: the PTSD data and the split (lines 31–33, 118–123)
ptsd <- read_csv("data/ptsd-for-knn.csv") |> mutate(ptsd = as.factor(ptsd))
n_ptsd <- nrow(ptsd)
prev_ptsd <- mean(ptsd$ptsd == "1")
set.seed(123)
ptsd_split <- initial_split(ptsd, prop = 0.75, strata = ptsd)
ptsd_train <- training(ptsd_split)
ptsd_test <- testing(ptsd_split)
ptsd_cv <- vfold_cv(ptsd_train, v = 5)
ptsd_cells <- ptsd |> group_by(anxiety, acute_stress) |> summarise(ptsd = mean(ptsd == 1), n = n(), .groups = "drop")
n_cells <- nrow(ptsd_cells)
# the simplest rule: the majority of your own cell (training set), scored on the test set
cell_rule <- ptsd_train |> group_by(anxiety, acute_stress) |> summarise(p = mean(ptsd == "1"), .groups = "drop")
cell_f1 <- ptsd_test |>
  left_join(cell_rule, by = c("anxiety", "acute_stress")) |>
  mutate(pred = factor(if_else(p > 0.5, "1", "0"), levels = c("0", "1"))) |>
  f_meas(truth = ptsd, estimate = pred, event_level = "second") |>
  pull(.estimate)
# the tutors' pre-fitted models (lines 61–77): decision boundaries for four values of k
knn_models <- read_rds("models/knn_models_output.R")
bounds <- knn_models |> unnest(grid)
cvm <- res$knn_cv_metrics
cvw <- cvm |> select(neighbors, .metric, mean) |> pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = mean)
cv_at <- function(k, m) cvw[[m]][cvw$neighbors == k]
best_k <- res$knn_best$neighbors
knn_train_f1 <- res$knn_train_f1$.estimate
knn_test_f1 <- res$knn_test_f1$.estimate
```

```{r}
#| label: visuals
#| include: false
# ---- Step-by-step visuals. Each helper draws the plot up to step k; the slide stacks one version per
# ---- step, so every click adds one element to the picture.

# Concept: a made-up cloud of people, two classes, and one new person. The k nearest get a circle and vote.
set.seed(7)
toy <- bind_rows(tibble(x = rnorm(22, 3.1, 1.1), y = rnorm(22, 3.0, 1.1), cls = "no"),
                 tibble(x = rnorm(18, 5.7, 1.1), y = rnorm(18, 5.5, 1.1), cls = "yes"))
newp <- tibble(x = 4.55, y = 4.35)
toy <- toy |> mutate(d = sqrt((x - newp$x)^2 + (y - newp$y)^2)) |> arrange(d)
toy_vote <- function(k) {
  v <- toy$cls[seq_len(k)]
  c(yes = sum(v == "yes"), no = sum(v == "no"))
}
knn_step <- function(k) {
  p <- ggplot(toy, aes(x, y)) +
    coord_fixed(xlim = c(0.5, 8.5), ylim = c(0.5, 8.3)) +
    theme_slide() +
    theme(legend.position = "right") +
    labs(x = "Feature 1", y = "Feature 2", colour = NULL)
  if (k > 0) {
    r <- toy$d[k] + 0.03
    circ <- tibble(t = seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 200)) |> mutate(x = newp$x + r * cos(t), y = newp$y + r * sin(t))
    v <- toy_vote(k)
    p <- p +
      geom_polygon(data = circ, fill = navy, alpha = 0.08) +
      geom_path(data = circ, colour = navy, linetype = "dashed") +
      geom_point(data = slice_head(toy, n = k), aes(colour = cls), size = 7, shape = 21, fill = NA, stroke = 1.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
      labs(title = paste0("k = ", k, ":  ", v["yes"], " yes, ", v["no"], " no  →  ", if (v["yes"] > v["no"]) "yes" else "no"))
  } else {
    p <- p + labs(title = "A new person. Yes or no?")
  }
  p + geom_point(aes(colour = cls), size = 3.2, alpha = 0.85) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(no = "#9E9E9E", yes = red), labels = c(no = "no", yes = "yes")) +
    geom_point(data = newp, shape = 23, size = 5.5, fill = "white", colour = navy, stroke = 1.8)
}

# The cross-validated metrics (Part I exercise, lines 181–195)
cv_plot <- function() {
  cvm |>
    mutate(neighbors = as.factor(neighbors),
           .metric = if_else(.metric == "f_meas", "F1-Score", str_to_title(.metric))) |>
    ggplot(aes(neighbors, mean, colour = .metric, group = .metric)) +
    geom_point(size = 2.5) +
    geom_line(linetype = "dashed") +
    scale_colour_bmj() +
    theme_slide() +
    theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()) +
    labs(x = "Number of neighbours (k)", y = "Mean cross-validated metric", colour = NULL)
}

# Part II concept: one feature, one outcome. Weekly childcare cost against median household income, training set.
cc1 <- childcare_train |> select(mhi_2018, mcsa)
set.seed(5)
cc1_s <- slice_sample(cc1, n = 2500)
inc_grid <- tibble(mhi_2018 = seq(min(cc1$mhi_2018), max(cc1$mhi_2018), length.out = 800))
tree1d <- function(depth, data = cc1, minbucket = 20) {
  rpart(mcsa ~ mhi_2018, data = data,
        control = rpart.control(maxdepth = depth, cp = 0, minsplit = 2 * minbucket, minbucket = minbucket, xval = 0))
}
pred_line <- function(fit, lab = "") inc_grid |> mutate(pred = predict(fit, inc_grid), lab = lab)
t1 <- tree1d(1); t2 <- tree1d(2); t3 <- tree1d(3)
t_deep <- tree1d(30, minbucket = 3)
cut1 <- t1$splits[1, "index"]
leaf1 <- t1$frame$yval[t1$frame$var == "<leaf>"]
cc_base <- function(pts = TRUE) {
  p <- ggplot(cc1_s, aes(mhi_2018, mcsa)) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k")) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(20000, 125000), ylim = c(20, 260)) +
    theme_slide() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 13)) +
    labs(x = "Median household income in the county", y = "Weekly childcare cost ($)",
         title = "One feature: each dot is a training county-year")
  if (pts) p <- p + geom_point(alpha = 0.18, size = 1.3, colour = grey)
  p
}
split_step <- function(k) {
  p <- cc_base()
  if (k >= 2) p <- p +
    geom_vline(xintercept = cut1, linetype = "dashed", colour = dark) +
    annotate("label", x = cut1, y = 250, label = paste0("income < ", dollar(cut1, scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k", accuracy = 0.1), "?"),
             colour = dark, fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
    geom_line(data = pred_line(t1), aes(y = pred), colour = red, linewidth = 1.6) +
    annotate("label", x = 30000, y = leaf1[1] - 20, label = paste0("mean: $", round(leaf1[1])), colour = red, fontface = "bold", size = 3.8) +
    annotate("label", x = 112000, y = leaf1[2] - 22, label = paste0("mean: $", round(leaf1[2])), colour = red, fontface = "bold", size = 3.8)
  if (k >= 3) p <- p + geom_line(data = pred_line(t2), aes(y = pred), colour = navy, linewidth = 1.4)
  if (k >= 4) p <- p + geom_line(data = pred_line(t3), aes(y = pred), colour = green, linewidth = 1.4)
  p
}
deep_step <- function(k) {
  p <- cc_base() + geom_line(data = pred_line(t3), aes(y = pred), colour = green, linewidth = 1.3)
  if (k >= 2) p <- p + geom_line(data = pred_line(t_deep), aes(y = pred), colour = red, linewidth = 0.8)
  p + labs(title = if (k >= 2) paste0("8 leaves (depth 3) against ", big(sum(t_deep$frame$var == "<leaf>")), " leaves") else "Depth 3 (8 leaves)")
}
# Bagging: three trees on three bootstrap samples, then the average of fifty
set.seed(11)
bag_trees <- map(1:3, ~ tree1d(4, data = slice_sample(cc1, prop = 1, replace = TRUE)))
bag_lines <- imap_dfr(bag_trees, ~ pred_line(.x, paste("Tree", .y)))
set.seed(12)
bag_avg <- map(1:50, ~ predict(tree1d(6, data = slice_sample(cc1, prop = 1, replace = TRUE), minbucket = 10), inc_grid)) |>
  reduce(`+`) / 50
bag_step <- function(k) {
  p <- cc_base()
  if (k >= 1 && k <= 3) p <- p + geom_line(data = filter(bag_lines, lab %in% paste("Tree", seq_len(k))), aes(y = pred, colour = lab), linewidth = 1.2)
  if (k >= 4) p <- p + geom_line(data = bag_lines, aes(y = pred, colour = lab), linewidth = 0.7, alpha = 0.6)
  if (k >= 5) p <- p + geom_line(data = mutate(inc_grid, pred = bag_avg), aes(y = pred), colour = red, linewidth = 1.8)
  p + scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Tree 1` = navy, `Tree 2` = green, `Tree 3` = "#8A5A00"), name = NULL) +
    labs(title = c("One tree, on a random resample of the counties", "A second resample, a second tree", "A third",
                   "Three trees, three different staircases", "The average of 50 such trees")[min(k, 5)])
}
# Boosting by hand: each round fits a small tree to what is left over, and adds a tenth of it
boost_1d <- function(rounds, lr = 0.1, depth = 2) {
  f <- rep(mean(cc1$mcsa), nrow(cc1)); g <- rep(mean(cc1$mcsa), nrow(inc_grid)); out <- list()
  for (r in seq_len(max(rounds))) {
    tr <- rpart(res ~ mhi_2018, data = mutate(cc1, res = mcsa - f),
                control = rpart.control(maxdepth = depth, cp = 0, minsplit = 40, minbucket = 20, xval = 0))
    f <- f + lr * predict(tr, cc1); g <- g + lr * predict(tr, inc_grid)
    if (r %in% rounds) out[[length(out) + 1]] <- inc_grid |> mutate(pred = g, rounds = r)
  }
  bind_rows(out)
}
boost_rounds <- c(1, 5, 20, 100)
boost_lines <- boost_1d(boost_rounds)
boost_step <- function(k) {
  d <- boost_lines |> filter(rounds <= boost_rounds[k]) |> mutate(rounds = factor(rounds))
  cc_base() +
    geom_line(data = d, aes(y = pred, colour = rounds, linewidth = rounds == boost_rounds[k])) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(c(pink, "#C95A66", dark, red), boost_rounds), name = "Trees so far") +
    scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 1.6, `FALSE` = 0.7), guide = "none") +
    labs(title = c("After 1 tree: a tenth of a step", "After 5", "After 20", "After 100 trees")[k])
}
```

::: {.ask}
You try 7 values of a knob, score each on the **test set**, keep the best, and report its test score. What's wrong?
:::

```{=html}
<div class="mcq">
  <div class="opt"><b>A</b>Nothing: that's what the test set is for</div>
  <div class="opt"><b>B</b>7 values is too few</div>
  <div class="opt right"><b>C</b>The test set helped choose the winner, so its score is no longer a fresh exam: it flatters</div>
  <div class="opt"><b>D</b>You should score on the training set instead</div>
  <div class="fragment why"><b>C.</b> Pick the best of 7 on the test set and you've used the test set for training decisions. The fix is to choose on the training data only, by <strong>cross-validation</strong>, and open the test set once, at the end. That's Part I.</div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
- Gauge: D is the Lab 4 instinct turned the wrong way. If many pick A, the folds slide needs the full 3 minutes.
- This is the organising idea of the day: three sets of rows with three jobs. Training rows fit; held-out folds of the training rows choose the knob; test rows judge once.

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[The vote]{.ct}
Majority wins. The share voting yes is `.pred_1`, as last week.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[k is yours to choose]{.ct}
1 neighbour says no, 5 say yes, 15 say no. **k is a hyperparameter.** Which k is right?
:::
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 2 minutes. A made-up cloud of people; grey = no, red = yes; the diamond is a new person.

- Click: one neighbour. The nearest person says "no". Click: five, and the vote flips to yes. Click: fifteen, and it flips back. Same data, same new person, three different answers: k matters.
- There is no fitting in the usual sense: the "model" is the training data itself. Predicting means searching it, which is why the tuning takes a while later.
- The recipe's step_normalize() is the only pre-processing: both features on the same scale so that the distance is fair.
:::

## The boundary depends on *k*

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Warm-up</span><span class="on">I · kNN + CV</span><span>II · Trees</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```


```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.6
bounds_plot()
```

::: {.cards .c3 style="margin-top:0.2em"}
::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact}
[Small k: jagged]{.ct}
With k = 100 and `r round(mean(ptsd_cells$n))` people per cell, the neighbours are mostly your **own cell**. The boundary follows each cell's quirks, and here it barely finds the "yes" region at all.
:::
:::
::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact}
[Large k: smooth]{.ct}
k = 1,000 pools several cells. The boundary is a broad diagonal band: "high anxiety **and** high stress".
:::
:::
::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[Which is right?]{.ct}
Not the picture's call. We need a **score for each k**, computed without touching the test set.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 2 minutes. These four models were fitted by the course team and saved; the notebook reads them from `models/knn_models_output.R` (line 61), so students don't wait for them. Shaded = predicted "yes".

- Left to right: k grows and the blue region grows into a smooth band. At k = 100 the shaded cells are the three top-right corners only: a quirk of ties, see the lesson plan, but the picture of "too few neighbours" is right.
- Too large a k would shade nothing or everything: with k = 33,000 every person has the same neighbours, the whole sample, and the vote is always "no" (66%). Somewhere in between is a sweet spot.
:::

## Choosing *k* without the test set: cross-validation {.nostretch}

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Warm-up</span><span class="on">I · kNN + CV</span><span>II · Trees</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="folds" style="--n:5">
  <div class="row head"><span class="lab"></span><i>fold 1</i><i>fold 2</i><i>fold 3</i><i>fold 4</i><i>fold 5</i><span class="sc">F1 for this k</span></div>
  <div class="row fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><span class="lab">Round 1</span><i class="hold">test</i><i>fit</i><i>fit</i><i>fit</i><i>fit</i><span class="sc">score 1</span></div>
  <div class="row fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><span class="lab">Round 2</span><i>fit</i><i class="hold">test</i><i>fit</i><i>fit</i><i>fit</i><span class="sc">score 2</span></div>
  <div class="row fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><span class="lab">Round 3</span><i>fit</i><i>fit</i><i class="hold">test</i><i>fit</i><i>fit</i><span class="sc">score 3</span></div>
  <div class="row fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><span class="lab">Round 4</span><i>fit</i><i>fit</i><i>fit</i><i class="hold">test</i><i>fit</i><span class="sc">score 4</span></div>
  <div class="row fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><span class="lab">Round 5</span><i>fit</i><i>fit</i><i>fit</i><i>fit</i><i class="hold">test</i><span class="sc">score 5</span></div>
  <div class="row sum fragment" data-fragment-index="3"><span class="lab"></span><i class="off"></i><i class="off"></i><i class="off"></i><i class="off"></i><i class="off"></i><span class="sc">mean of the 5</span></div>
</div>
```

::: {.cards .c3 style="margin-top:0.5em"}
::: {.card .compact}
[The training set, cut into 5 folds]{.ct}
`vfold_cv(ptsd_train, v = 5)`. The **test set is not in the picture**: it stays sealed until the very end.
:::
::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[Five rounds]{.ct}
Each round fits on 4 folds and scores on the 5th. Every row is held out exactly once. Five "mini test sets", none of them the real one.
:::
:::
::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[One number per k]{.ct}
Average the five scores. Repeat for every k on the list; keep the k with the best average. Then, once, the test set.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Timing: 3 minutes. This is the slide to get right; everything in the code block implements it.

- Click: round one, fold 1 is the mini test set. Click: the other four rounds. Click: the mean. That mean is what `collect_metrics()` reports as `mean`, with `n = 5` and a standard error.
- Why not just one held-out piece? One split is noisy: it depends on which rows landed where. Five scores averaged are steadier, and every row gets to be tested.
- Cost: 5 fits per candidate k. 4 candidates today, so 20 fits before the final one.
- "k-fold" uses k for the number of folds in textbooks; today k is the number of neighbours and v (`v = 5`) is the number of folds. Say it once to avoid the mix-up.
:::

## Model, recipe, workflow

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Warm-up</span><span class="on">I · kNN + CV</span><span>II · Trees</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="nbref"><b>Notebook</b> lines 130–150 <span>the model at line 132, the recipe at 142, the workflow at 146</span><i>code together</i></p>
```

::: {.anatomy}
```{=html}
<p class="anat-code" style="font-size:0.5em">knn_model &lt;- <span class="tok">nearest_neighbor(</span>neighbors = <span class="tok">tune()</span>) |&gt;
  <span class="tok">set_mode("classification")</span> |&gt; set_engine("kknn")

knn_rec &lt;- <span class="tok">recipe(ptsd ~ ., data = ptsd_train)</span> |&gt;
  <span class="tok">step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())</span>

wf_knn &lt;- <span class="tok">workflow()</span> |&gt; add_model(knn_model) |&gt; add_recipe(knn_rec)</p>
```

1. **Which kind of model**, like `linear_reg()` and `logistic_reg()`.
2. **A placeholder**: "cross-validation fills this in". Warm-up 1's knob.
3. **Say the job.** kNN can classify or predict a number; `kknn` does the work.
4. **A recipe**: the formula **plus** the pre-processing to run before fitting.
5. **Same scale for both features** (mean 0, SD 1), so distance is fair.
6. **Bundle model and recipe.** `fit()` on a workflow runs both; predictions get the same recipe.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Two new objects. A **recipe** is pre-processing written down as steps, applied inside the fitting, so the test set gets exactly the same treatment later. A **workflow** holds the recipe and the model together, so one `fit()` does both and nothing is forgotten.
- Nothing has been fitted yet: all three objects are descriptions. Print `wf_knn` to see "Model: nearest_neighbor(), neighbors = tune()".
- `all_numeric_predictors()` picks every numeric feature; the outcome is left alone.
:::

## Metrics, candidates, and the tuning run

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Warm-up</span><span class="on">I · kNN + CV</span><span>II · Trees</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="nbref"><b>Notebook</b> lines 154–175 <span>metrics and grid at 156–160, <code>tune_grid()</code> at 167</span><i>code together</i></p>
```

::: {.anatomy}
```{=html}
<p class="anat-code" style="font-size:0.5em">class_metrics &lt;- <span class="tok">metric_set(recall, precision, f_meas)</span>
grid_knn &lt;- <span class="tok">tibble(neighbors = c(100, 500, 1000, 3000))</span>
<span class="tok">doParallel::registerDoParallel()</span>

knn_model_cv &lt;- <span class="tok">tune_grid(</span>wf_knn, <span class="tok">resamples = ptsd_cv</span>,
    metrics = class_metrics, grid = grid_knn,
    <span class="tok">control = control_resamples(event_level = "second")</span>)</p>
```

1. **Three scores**, as in Lab 4. We pick by F1.
2. **The candidates**: one column per knob, one row per value to try.
3. **Use all the cores**: the fits can run side by side.
4. **Every candidate on every fold: fit, score.** 4 × 5 = 20 fits.
5. **The five rounds** from the folds slide.
6. **Score the 1s**, as last week, passed through `control`.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Run it, then wait: about 2½ minutes on a laptop, longer on Nuvolos. The notebook says "put on the kettle". While it runs, next slide.
- The result `knn_model_cv` holds 20 fits' worth of scores; `collect_metrics()` averages them per k. That's the exercise.
- event_level: same trap as last week. Without it, recall and precision are computed for the 0s.
:::

```{=html}
</div>
```

::: {.column width="54%"}
::: {.card .compact}
[Cross-validation did its job]{.ct}
It ranked the candidates on training rows only, and its score for the winner matched the test set. The test set was opened once.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[Why large k won]{.ct}
Every dot is a cell of `r round(mean(ptsd_cells$n))` people. k = 100 can't see past its own cell; k = `r big(best_k)` averages a neighbourhood of cells. With two 0–10 features, **the cell majority is already as good as it gets**: F1 `r f3(cell_f1)`.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[kNN has no coefficients]{.ct}
Nothing to read off, no "per unit of anxiety". Flexible, and slow to predict. Trees, next, are flexible **and** readable.
:::
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Debrief, 5 minutes.

- The three bars are the three jobs from warm-up 2: fit on training rows, choose on held-out folds of them, judge on the test set. All three agree because the model is coarse (two features, large k): little room to memorise.
- The "simplest rule" line is a reality check: on this data a lookup table of 121 cells does as well as the tuned kNN. That is not a failure of kNN; it's what two integer features allow.
- The k = 100 collapse is partly technical: the `kknn` engine weights neighbours by distance, and in a cell of 100+ identical people every distance is zero, so its weights break down and it predicts "no". A plain majority vote (`set_engine("kknn", kernel = "rectangular")`) does better at k = 100 but still worse than 1,000. The lesson is unchanged: too few neighbours, too jagged.
:::

## How a tree splits

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Warm-up</span><span class="done">I · kNN + CV</span><span class="on">II · Trees</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

:::: {.columns style="align-items:start"}

::: {.r-stack}

:::
:::
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
::: {.card .compact}
[One yes/no question]{.ct}
Two groups, each predicted by its **mean**. Of every cut on every feature, keep the one that **cuts the squared error most**.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[Ask again inside each group]{.ct}
Depth 2: four groups, four means. Each cut is the best **for its own group**: greedy, no look-ahead.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[A staircase, not a line]{.ct}
Depth 3: eight steps. A prediction is the mean of the **leaf** you land in. With 50 features, each question can use a different one.
:::
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Timing: the tree concept block is 10 minutes across this slide and the next three: splits 3, overfitting 2, forests 3, boosting 2.

- Click: one cut. The tree looked at every possible cut point and chose the one whose two means fit best. Click: it repeats inside each half. Click: and again.
- A tree is a flow chart of questions; the drawing at the exercise is exactly that. Reading it needs no statistics, which is why trees are popular with people who have to explain a decision.
- Greedy: the first question is the best single question, not the best start of a plan. That's why trees can be unstable: a slightly different data set can change the first cut and everything below it.
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}
One tree is **unstable**: resample, and the staircase moves.

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
::: {.card .compact}
[Bagging: average many trees]{.ct}
Resample the rows, grow a tree, repeat, **average**. Different wobbles cancel.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[Random forest: + random features]{.ct}
Each split picks from only `mtry` ≈ 7 **random features**, so the trees stop copying each other.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[The price]{.ct}
1,000 trees can't be read: predictions and a ranking, no picture.
:::
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
- Click: a second tree on a second resample; click: a third. Three staircases, three different sets of steps. Click: the average of fifty is a smooth curve that no single tree could draw.
- Why random features too? With income in every tree's first split, the trees would all look alike and the averaging would gain little. Forcing variety is what makes the forest better than plain bagging.
- `rand_forest(mtry = 7, trees = 1000)` in the exercise is exactly this. The notebook writes `round(sqrt(52), 0)`; the data has 50 features, and both round to 7.
:::

- Click: the real XGBoost on all 50 features. The test RMSE drops fast over the first hundred trees and then flattens. With more trees or a bigger learning rate it would start climbing: the folds from the next slide are how you would find the stopping point.
- XGBoost is the version of boosting that wins most tabular-data competitions; `boost_tree()` with `set_engine("xgboost")` is all the exercise needs.
:::

## Split by time

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Warm-up</span><span class="done">I · kNN + CV</span><span class="on">II · Trees</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="nbref"><b>Notebook</b> lines 265–291 <span>the split at 265, the folds at 280; skip the callout at 293–354</span><i>code together</i></p>
```

:::: {.columns style="align-items:start"}

::: {.column width="54%"}
::: {.anatomy .one}
```{=html}
<p class="anat-code" style="font-size:0.46em">childcare_train &lt;- childcare |&gt;
  <span class="tok">filter(study_year &lt;= 2016)</span> |&gt; arrange(study_year) |&gt;
  <span class="tok">mutate(study_date = as.Date(paste0(study_year, "-01-01")))</span>
childcare_test &lt;- childcare |&gt; filter(study_year &gt; 2016) |&gt; mutate(…)

childcare_cv &lt;- <span class="tok">sliding_period(</span>childcare_train,
  index = study_date, period = "year",
  <span class="tok">lookback = Inf, assess_stop = 1</span>, step = 1)</p>
```

1. **Split by year, not at random**: 2008–2016 to train, 2017–2018 to test, so no 2017 row teaches the model about 2017.
2. **A real date column**: the folds function wants one.
3. **Folds that respect time**: fit on the past, score the next year.
4. **Expanding window**: all earlier years in, one year out. 8 rounds.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}
```{=html}
<div class="folds" style="--n:11;font-size:0.5em">
  <div class="row head"><span class="lab"></span><i>08</i><i>09</i><i>10</i><i>11</i><i>12</i><i>13</i><i>14</i><i>15</i><i>16</i><i>17</i><i>18</i><span class="sc"></span></div>

</div>
```

## A recipe with roles

```{=html}
<div class="tracker"><span class="done">Warm-up</span><span class="done">I · kNN + CV</span><span class="on">II · Trees</span><span>Wrap-up</span></div>
```

```{=html}
<p class="nbref"><b>Notebook</b> lines 358–363 <span>one recipe, shared by all three models</span><i>code together</i></p>
```

::: {.anatomy}
```{=html}
<p class="anat-code" style="font-size:0.6em">childcare_rec &lt;-
  <span class="tok">recipe(mcsa ~ ., data = childcare_train)</span> |&gt;
  <span class="tok">update_role(starts_with(c("county", "state")), new_role = "id")</span> |&gt;
  update_role(c("study_date", "study_year"), new_role = "id")</p>
```

1. **Cost against everything else.** `.` means every other column: `r n_feat` features, plus six columns that shouldn't be.
2. **Keep but don't use.** County and state names, the FIPS code, the year and the date become `id` columns: they stay in the table as labels and **out of the model**. Without this the model would use the county code as a number.
:::

::: {.cards .c2 style="margin-top:0.5em"}
::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact}
[No normalising this time]{.ct}
Trees ask "is income below $47.7k?", and a cut-off doesn't care about scale. The kNN recipe needed `step_normalize()`; this one doesn't.
:::
:::
::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[One recipe, three models]{.ct}
Tasks 1–3 add this recipe to three different workflows. Change the recipe once and all three models change with it.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- Type lines 359–362. The recipe is the same object as in Part I, with roles instead of a normalising step.
- Why no normalising: a tree's question compares one feature with a cut-off, so the units don't matter. Distance-based methods (kNN) need it; tree-based ones don't.
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}

[The first question]{.ct}
`one_race_a < `r f1(first_split)``, the share of Asian residents: a **proxy** for expensive metro counties, not a cause.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[Then income, households, women's jobs]{.ct}

[What the model is]{.ct}
Eight numbers, one per leaf, $`r round(min(res$dt_rpart$frame$yval))` to $`r round(max(res$dt_rpart$frame$yval))`. Everyone in a leaf gets the same price: hence RMSE $`r round(dt_test)`.

::::

::: {.notes}
Discuss, 2 minutes. Take the notebook's two questions in turn.

- Read the first box aloud: 100% of counties, mean $99. "Is the Asian share below 2.2%?" Yes goes left (87% of counties), no goes right. Ask what that variable stands for: it is not a cause of childcare prices; it marks the big coastal metro areas where everything is expensive. Trees take whatever splits best.
- The notebook's answer names the same five variables and calls `one_race_a` the most important because it splits first. Add: "first" and "most important" are not quite the same; the forest's permutation importance puts income first.
:::


:::: {.yt}

::: {.tasks}
[Part II · Tasks 2–4 · lines 399–504]{.lbl}

1. **Lines 404–421, Task 2:** a `rand_forest()` with `mtry = round(sqrt(52), 0)` and `trees = 1e3`, engine `ranger`; fit; score both sets
2. **Line 424:** better predictions? Overfitting?
3. **Lines 431–457, Task 3:** a `boost_tree()` with the same `mtry`, `trees = 1000`, `learn_rate = 0.1`, engine `xgboost`; fit; score
4. **Lines 468–504, Task 4:** one table of test RMSE for the three models, and a bar chart
:::

::: {.cheat}
[Three specs, one pattern]{.lbl}

```r
rf_model <-
  rand_forest(mtry = round(sqrt(52), 0), trees = 1e3) |>
  set_mode("regression") |>
  set_engine("ranger", num.threads = parallel::detectCores() - 1)

xgb_model <-
  boost_tree(mtry = round(sqrt(52), 0), trees = 1000,
             learn_rate = 0.1) |>
  set_mode("regression") |>
  set_engine("xgboost", nthread = parallel::detectCores() - 1)
# then workflow() |> add_recipe() |> add_model() |> fit(), as Task 1

list("Decision Tree" = dt_fit, "Random Forest" = rf_fit,
     "XGBoost" = xgb_fit) |>                      # Task 4
  map_dfr(~ augment(.x, new_data = childcare_test),
          .id = "model") |>          # list names → a column
  group_by(model) |>
  regress_metrics(mcsa, .pred) |>    # one score per model
  filter(.metric == "rmse")
```

::: {.stuck}
**Stuck?** The forest takes 20–30 s, XGBoost a few: normal. The bar chart is `geom_col()` + `coord_flip()`
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Your turn, 9 minutes. Tasks 2 and 3 are Task 1 with a different model function and engine; Task 4 is Lab 4's `map_dfr()` over a list of fitted models instead of a list of thresholds.

- The notebook's XGBoost spec also passes `eval_metric = "rmse"` to the engine; it only affects what xgboost prints while training. The sheet leaves it out.
- Fast finishers: `extract_fit_engine(rf_fit)` with `importance = "permutation"` in set_engine() for a feature ranking; or tune `learn_rate` with `tune()` and `tune_grid(…, resamples = childcare_cv)`.
:::

## Solutions: Tasks 2 and 3 {.solution}

:::: {.walk .dense}

::: {.walk-code}
```r
rf_model <-
  rand_forest(mtry = round(sqrt(52), 0), trees = 1e3) |>
  set_mode("regression") |>
  set_engine("ranger", num.threads = parallel::detectCores() - 1)

rf_fit <- workflow() |> add_recipe(childcare_rec) |>
  add_model(rf_model) |> fit(data = childcare_train)

rf_fit |> augment(new_data = childcare_train) |> regress_metrics(mcsa, .pred)
rf_fit |> augment(new_data = childcare_test)  |> regress_metrics(mcsa, .pred)

xgb_model <-
  boost_tree(mtry = round(sqrt(52), 0), trees = 1000,
             learn_rate = 0.1) |>
  set_mode("regression") |>
  set_engine("xgboost", nthread = parallel::detectCores() - 1,
             eval_metric = "rmse")

xgb_fit <- workflow() |> add_recipe(childcare_rec) |>
  add_model(xgb_model) |> fit(data = childcare_train)

xgb_fit |> augment(new_data = childcare_train) |> regress_metrics(mcsa, .pred)
xgb_fit |> augment(new_data = childcare_test)  |> regress_metrics(mcsa, .pred)
```

::: {.walk-say}
The forest, then the boosted trees. Same workflow, same scores.
:::
:::

::: {.walk-out}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=0 lines="1-7"}
::: {.say}
1,000 trees, each on a resample of the rows, each split choosing among 7 random features. `num.threads` uses all cores but one; it takes about 20 seconds.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
cat("== Workflow [trained] ==================\nPreprocessor: Recipe\nModel: rand_forest()\n\nRanger result\n\n  Type:                 Regression\n  Number of trees:      1000\n  Mtry:                 7\n  Target node size:     5\n  Variable importance mode: none\n  ...")
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1 lines="9-10"}
::: {.say}
Training RMSE `r f1(rf_train)` against test `r f1(rf_test)`: the forest fits its own rows almost perfectly and the test set much better than the tree (`r f1(dt_test)`). R² on the test set `r f2(rf_rsq)`.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
res$rf_metrics |> mutate(.estimate = round(.estimate, 3))
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2 lines="12-20"}
::: {.say}
1,000 small trees in sequence, each adding a tenth of its correction. A few seconds.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
cat("== Workflow [trained] ==================\nPreprocessor: Recipe\nModel: boost_tree()\n\nMain Arguments:\n  mtry = 7\n  trees = 1000\n  learn_rate = 0.1\n\nComputational engine: xgboost\n  ...")
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3 lines="22-23"}
::: {.say}
Test RMSE `r f1(xgb_test)`, the best of the three; training `r f1(xgb_train)`, the same big gap as the forest. R² `r f2(xgb_rsq)`.
:::

```{r}

res$xgb_metrics |> mutate(.estimate = round(.estimate, 3))
```
:::

Each click highlights the next step of the code, shows the result, and explains it below the code. The two model printouts are shortened; the metrics are shown as one table per model (set, metric, estimate) rather than two.

## Solutions: Task 4 {.solution}

:::: {.walk}

::: {.walk-code}
```r
model_results <-
  list(
    "Decision Tree" = dt_fit,
    "Random Forest" = rf_fit,
    "XGBoost"       = xgb_fit
  ) |>
  map_dfr(~ .x |> augment(new_data = childcare_test),
          .id = "model") |>
  group_by(model) |>
  regress_metrics(mcsa, .pred) |>
  filter(.metric == "rmse")

ggplot(model_results,
       aes(x = reorder(model, .estimate),
           y = .estimate, fill = model)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(.estimate, 1)),
            hjust = -0.1) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "RMSE (lower is better)")
```

::: {.walk-say}
Score the three fits on the test set in one go, then draw the result.
:::
:::

::: {.walk-out}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=0 lines="1-11"}
::: {.say}
`map_dfr()` runs `augment()` on each fit and stacks the three tables; `.id` keeps the list names. `group_by(model)` then gives one RMSE per model.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
res$model_results |> filter(.metric == "rmse") |> mutate(.estimate = round(.estimate, 2))
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1 lines="13-20"}
::: {.say}
`reorder()` sorts the bars by RMSE; `coord_flip()` turns them sideways so the names fit. The notebook adds a title, theme and colours.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.4
#| fig-height: 3.2
res$model_results |>
  filter(.metric == "rmse") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(model, .estimate), y = .estimate, fill = model)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE, width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(.estimate, 1)), hjust = -0.15, size = 4.5, fontface = "bold") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`Decision Tree` = grey, `Random Forest` = navy, XGBoost = red)) +
  expand_limits(y = 36) +
  theme_slide() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Test-set RMSE (lower is better)")
```
:::
:::

```{=html}
<p class="tbl-cap">Test-set RMSE <small>dollars a week; lower is better</small></p>
<div class="bars">
  <div><span>predict the mean</span><i style="width:`r round(100 * base_rmse / 40)`%;background:#BDBDBD"></i><b>`r f1(base_rmse)`</b></div>
  <div><span>one tree</span><i style="width:`r round(100 * dt_test / 40)`%"></i><b>`r f1(dt_test)`</b></div>
  <div><span>random forest</span><i class="hot" style="width:`r round(100 * rf_test / 40)`%"></i><b>`r f1(rf_test)`</b></div>
  <div><span>XGBoost</span><i class="hot" style="width:`r round(100 * xgb_test / 40)`%"></i><b>`r f1(xgb_test)`</b></div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="calc sm" style="margin-top:0.8em">
  <div><span class="cl">Train → test</span><span class="cx">tree `r f1(dt_train)` → `r f1(dt_test)` <small>small gap</small></span></div>
  <div><span class="cl"></span><span class="cx">forest `r f1(rf_train)` → `r f1(rf_test)` <small>large gap</small></span></div>
  <div class="hl"><span class="cl"></span><span class="cx">XGBoost `r f1(xgb_train)` → `r f1(xgb_test)` <small>large gap, best test score</small></span></div>
</div>
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.card .compact}
[Many trees beat one]{.ct}
The ensembles cut the tree's error by a quarter and explain `r round(100 * xgb_rsq)`% of the variance in test-year prices against the tree's `r round(100 * dt_rsq)`%.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact .line}
[Mind the gap]{.ct}
A training RMSE of $`r round(rf_train)` means the forest has nearly memorised 2008–2016. The honest number is the test one. Part of the gap is also **time**: prices rose in 2017–2018, and the models have never seen those years.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.card .compact .dark}
[Nothing was tuned]{.ct}
1,000 trees, `mtry` 7, learning rate 0.1: defaults and rules of thumb. Part I's recipe, `tune()` plus the time folds, is how you'd do better.
:::
:::
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Debrief, 2 minutes. The notebook's two discussion questions (lines 424 and 460) in one picture.

- "Does the forest help with overfitting?" The notebook's answer says the train–test discrepancy is larger than the tree's. True, and worth being precise about: a forest's training error is always tiny, because each row was in most trees' resamples; it says little about overfitting. The test RMSE is what to compare, and there the forest wins clearly.
- The test years are harder: the median price rose from $100 in 2016 to $106 in 2018, so a model trained on the past under-predicts. A random split would have hidden that and flattered every model.
- If asked which to use: XGBoost by the numbers, the single tree if you must explain each prediction to a parent or a council.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="checks" style="grid-template-columns:1fr">
  <div><b>1</b><span>A <strong>hyperparameter</strong> is a setting you choose, not one <code>fit()</code> estimates: the number of neighbours, the depth of a tree, the number of trees, the learning rate. Choose it by <strong>cross-validation</strong>: cut the training set into folds, score every candidate on held-out folds, average, pick. The <strong>test set stays sealed</strong> until the end. In code: <code>vfold_cv()</code>, <code>tune()</code>, <code>tune_grid()</code>, <code>select_best()</code>, <code>finalize_workflow()</code></span></div>
  <div><b>2</b><span><strong>k nearest neighbours</strong> lets the k closest training rows vote: small k is jagged, large k is smooth. A <strong>decision tree</strong> asks one yes/no question at a time and predicts the mean of the leaf: readable, unstable, and it overfits if grown too far</span></div>
  <div><b>3</b><span><strong>Ensembles</strong> fix the tree's instability. A <strong>random forest</strong> averages many trees grown on resampled rows with random features; <strong>boosting</strong> adds small trees that each correct the last. Both beat one tree; neither can be read like one</span></div>
</div>
```

**Question:** you have the 2019 prices. Which model do you deploy, and how would you check whether the forest's training RMSE of $`r round(rf_train)` means anything?

::: {.notes}
Wrap-up, 4 minutes.

- Recap in three sentences.
- Exit question on Moodle: XGBoost by test RMSE; the training RMSE means almost nothing for an ensemble, so score 2019 (a new year) and compare with the 2017–2018 test score.
:::
